Once you are over 500M and we know it is not CVC it normally comes down to three things:

1) Local equipment – could be a router doing something, a wifi test.
2) testing in web browser – use the speed test app, makes a massive difference
3) which test server are you using. Try an alternative server.

It's really a question of trying to get the most from your connection.

Connexa writes...

Given I’m getting good upload on my WiFi testing I suspect my mikrotik is configured right.

Cut over from FTTC to FTTP (250/25) jumping from Telstra to Leaptel around May last year.
Initial speed tests were good (around 269 DL and initially saw 29 upload, tho that dropped down to around 18/19 testing from PC (ethernet).

Just before Christmas, did a speed test from PC – 269 DL but only 8 UL. Speedtests from the router itself and a number of wireless devices (ipad and Samsung phone) had similar DL speeds but UL of about 22/23. Subsequent tests from PC varied greatly for UL speed, but generally only about half of what was expected.

Checked drivers etc. , tried different ethernet cable, connected PC direct to UNI-D port of NTD, and UL speeds still slow – suspect PC?. Tried a 'SpeedOf Me' test from PC which returned an UL speed of 26 (and max of about 27). The time graphs tho did show that there were a number of dips on both DL and UL speeds.

Yesterday set up Bandwidth Limiter in QoS settings of router for the PC of 245 DL and 24 UL.
Speed test from PC now around 21-23 for UL

Odd that UL speeds were generally not too bad at the beginning – perhaps NBN have became more stringent with their policer.
It was confusing how issue only appeared using the PC via ethernet, but wireless devices were no problem – but all seems good now even tho SpeedOfMe graphs still show dips (latest test was 238.8 DL (max 257) and 25.6 UL(max 28.5).

the1+ writes...

my best option is to buy a switch that sits between the NTD and my router and set up a upload limit only.

Where ever you have heard or read that.. forget it as that is some very poor advice IMO..

First things first you need to understand the difference between a shaper and policer – https://networkexpert.co/blog/trafficpolicevstrafficshape.html#:~:text=Queueing%20is%20an%20outbound%20concept,transmission%20of%20any%20delayed%20packets.

Most switches use a policer which is very harsh on the traffic flow which as you can see causes a saw tooth like traffic graph due to how harsh it is on the traffic flow.

What you are wanting to enable on your router is an upload shaper. Unfortunately having a connection like 1000/50 (connection being so asymmetrical) can cause some issues without one enabled like your seeing plus NBN have very harsh policers on their network too..

I hope this is of some help to you understanding what is really going on with your upload speeds with your connection.

Lukesky77 writes...

yes thanks for the feedback, might have to revisit plans if i am not getting those speeds on my devices – didnt realise i needed powerful devices to get 1gb speeds. Need to read the fine print again...

Its kinda up to you to ensure your devices can harness the power of the internet connection you have... all the RSP can really do is give you the speed to the network boundary point. From there it falls upon us as individuals to make good use of it.

With that said, even though an individual device may not be getting 1Gbps, its worth considering whether across your internet use in your household does 1Gbps benefit you.

Eg. You're downloading something on the playstation at "only" 500Mbps, meanwhile someone else is watching youtube, your security cameras are going etc. If you're only on a 250Mbps plan then your playstation will chew up the entire bandwidth.

The app or speedtest-cli is "closer to metal" code. Running through the browser has some layers of code that it has to go through, then there's extensions and the different browser engines which you can expect all behave differently.
In my experience, a powerful machine will produce the same results on the web and on the app and consistently so.
But a low performance machine will produce much higher and more consistent results via the app because of the native code.

CDogg writes...

Yeah I would leave Download at 0 or the highest whichever makes it uncapped (can't remember), these consumer boxes aren't good at capping download speeds.

There’s two shaper / policers before your router. That being the ISPs and them nbn’s. So if your router was in some way able to impact your download speed it wouldn’t have any positive impact. There’s nothing between the router and your devices on download.

On upload, your isp can’t shape it between your router and nbn as they sit on the other side of nbn. So if you don’t shape your own traffic you hit nbn’s policer which drops packets resulting in bad speedtest results. So if you can shape your traffic to be just under the nbn policer you will get much more consistent speedtest results.

Sorry I worded that wrong, I meant yeah it's conservative in general – that is the QoS implementation on the TP-Links.
In terms of the download though, you will get worse results than when using it for upload because the router needs more processing power especially when shaping in the hundreds of Mbps.

It would be highly unusual for me to have more than one device using lots of bandwidth, especially upload. But if it may burst after sustained uploads even from a single device then that would be an issue.

IIRC, when I tested on them for a saturated link both download + upload at the same time, with 2 concurrent clients, you can get it to burst at that point which is when you will see the spike. So I opted to follow what they said on the tin, that is to put the speed in as "as per your internet provider" or whatever it said.
I figured from that and the resulting speed, that they are already negating some from the value you input for TCP overhead and the usual ~%5 buffer you need to leave when setting QoS filters.
Other brands/implementations need you to calculate and put that buffer in yourself.

ChickenChowMein writes...

Just upgraded to Leaptel 1000/50 FTTP last night and I’m only getting 650/47 on the router connected directly to the NTD through wifi. This drops to about 250-350 when connected to the satellites on my mesh network. For those getting 900+ speeds are you connected through Ethernet or wifi?

Also would I be right in saying that I’ll never get close to 1000 speeds with my equipment which is limited to wifi 5?

650Mbps on WiFi5 is good. Wi-Fi6 will get you closer to ~800-900 depending on how close you are to the main router node and how good your device is. And that's assuming using a 80Mhz channel. If using 160Mhz you could theoretically get 1Gbps+. WiFi 6E even more.

There are lots of variables involved that I don't want to derail this thread with.

Getting ~250-350 on the nodes is normal for WiFi backhaul of a WiFi5 system, even for a budget WiFi6 mesh system. Again there are lots of variables in play with this.

Finally, yes, most people you see showcasing the 900+ speeds are testing via Ethernet even if they may use Wi-Fi 90% of the time.

H4kunaMatata writes...

What is the problem with fast.com ?

Well, the physical port doesn't go faster than 1 Gbps. And the overhead in TCP brings down the maximum to about 940 Mbps. So any speedtest result (fast.com or otherwise) that shows more than that is blatantly inaccurate.

I get similar results from fast.com (https://ibb.co/XYQbSdM), but I know it's wrong.

You should look at tests like this: https://www.waveform.com/tools/bufferbloat

Speed is one thing, but what you'll notice more is if latency increases when the connection is under load (often referred to as "bufferbloat").

OPNsense has options to decrease bufferbloat. (see: https://docs.opnsense.org/manual/how-tos/shaper_bufferbloat.html)

My router (EdgeRouter 4) is only powerful enough to do fq_codel in the upload direction, and you can see that is very well controlled. (I.e., latency doesn't increase even when upload is being fully utilized).

But when download is being fully utilized, my latency increases +8ms. All things considered, that's not bad. But if your router can do fq_codel at gigabit speeds, you can bring that down to +0ms. (OPNsense on decent hardware can do this.)

cool1 writes...

Synology WRX530

Do you have "Threat Prevention" or "Parental Controls" enabled? If so, disable these as a test. They may not support gigabit speeds.

If you have Windows and/or Android client devices, you can try enabling the 160 MHz channel width on 5 GHz channel in your Synology. There are potential downsides, but it can lead to faster overall throughput if that's what you're chasing.(Apple clients won't make use of the extra channel width, so there's no benefit if you're running Apple clients.). [edit: It appears the Synology doesn't support 160 MHz channel width.]

Generally speaking, I'd advise against using 160 MHz channel width for the 5 GHz network. But it's an option to experiment with.

cool1 writes...

My Laptop is wifi 6

What laptop (or wifi network card)? What connection speed is the wifi network adapter reporting? (E.g., on a Mac, you can Option-click the WiFi menu icon, and it will show you details about the connection, including the Tx Rate.) Note that this speed is the WiFi connection rate, and due to overheads in how WiFi works, your actual throughput is going to be somewhere between 50%-75% of this value.

Checked through the phone samsung s24 Ultra

580 Mbps over WiFi 6 isn't terrible. Can probably do a bit better, but it's going to require you to be close to the router, with no neighbouring interference, and no other traffic on your network. As mentioned above, 160 MHz channel width could help here. To get the fastest possible speeds from the Samsung, you need a router that supports WiFi 7 and 6 GHz networks. (The devices you listed do not support this.)

Ray1977 writes...

but upload still 18.9 maxed out see below

Your upload will remain at 20M until you remove the sim card and factory reset your device. This is because the unit will connect to Telstra and see what was the previous telstra service on it and set a shaper limiting the upload based on that value. The setting is not accessible to change and a factory reset is the only way to fix it.

Exposure2010 writes...

I may look at a range extender. Got my eye on the TP-Link RE705X AX3000.

Careful. A range extender of that nature is unlikely to net you much improvement, in fact likely to net you a loss.
Range extenders like that one effectively half the connection speed that it can get at the location it's installed at.
Wi-Fi is a half duplex communication medium, meaning it needs to transmit and receive at the same time (on the same "lane")

Spudling writes...

how do mesh units not sacrifice speed if they are using wifi capacity to mesh?

They will sacrifice speed similarly if they're dual-band mesh units. But if they're tri-band then it will be better in-theory. but not always the case.
Saying that, something like the Eero 6+ while dual-band uses 160Mhz to mesh, so tends to get good results because you're looking at up to ~2400Mbps on the 160Mhz band. (of course that's without getting into the usual loses and so on so forth that I won't get into here..)

All in all, I think the point is it is very hard to get close to 1Gbps capacity all over your house unless you are wiring APs in with proper planning along with the correct hardware. Most good Wi-Fi 6 router/AP combos will be be able to get close to 1Gbps when close to it (with an equivalently capable device) but will fall short with distance quite quickly.

Remode writes...

Ping 7ms | Download 57ms | Upload 9ms.

These are measures of latency under load. This is the kind of thing you "feel" more than raw speed. Often talked about under the heading of "buffer bloat". Those aren't terrible results. Normally, the way you deal with that is by implementing some kind of QoS or SQM on your router. (e.g., on UniFi routers, the "Smart Queues" feature will mitigate buffer bloat.) The hard part is that this is CPU-intensive, especially for faster internet speeds. But properly configured, you can achieve results where the ping while idle, ping while downloading, and ping while uploading is all the same.

There are tests that are dedicated to measuring buffer bloat, such as: https://www.waveform.com/tools/bufferbloat

--KK-- writes...

Opticomm estate congestion? What the hell is that?

Can be congestion on the particular GPON segment (remembering GPON is a shared medium and Opticomm tech specs allow up to 64 premises/segment sharing 2.488Gbps bandwidth) or congestion on the link between the estate OLT and the Opticomm POI eg they may only have a 10Gbps or if an older OLT may only have say 4*1G links.

Some of the ex Telstra velocity estates, under Telstra times were so congested they could barely achieve double digit Mbps and there were stop sells on 100Mbps services.

rk writes...

I was on 100/20 HFC plan. Now 500/50 . Speed tests showed 160 to 225 downloads. I kicked the session and rebooted router and NBN modem. Still 160/45.

Slow PC or slow router can cause results like that. What speed do you get if you plug straight into the NTD?
If you get the expected speed then you computer is fast enough and the router is the bottle neck. If its the same then its possible the PC isn't faster enough, or there is an actual fault on the NBN. If you check task manager and look at the performance tab , if CPU is doing 100% then its a slow PC issue.

hayythere writes...

Unifi Cloud Gateway Ultra

Look for "Smart Queues". Should be under Settings > Internet > {your internet} > Smart Queues

Is it enabled and set to anything right now?

I would enable it, set Downrate to 0 Mbps, Uprate to 47 Mbps. (You can experiment, but start there. Setting the Downrate to 0 means it isn't applying Smart Queues in that direction — which is what you want.)

Save the settings and let it provision.

Then run your test again.

(Note: On the same page, there's an "Expected ISP Speeds" setting. That is strictly for reporting/graphing purposes. You can put something like 540 down, 47 up, but it won't have any impact on your actual connection.)
